1.evidence: Section 1 defines both outcomes, uses the 1960 and 1985 endpoints for growth per working-age person, and explains the overlapping samples of 98, 75 and 22 countries. Sections 3 and 5 state the separate identification assumptions for levels and transitions. Section 5 explains why persistent efficiency is especially consequential when initial income is a regressor. The country appendix labels units, flags and missing cells.

2.evidence: Section 2 derives the stationary stocks and proves convergence from positive initial stocks. Tables 1–4 report coefficients, standard errors, adjusted fit, residual scales and dilution-restriction tests. The auxiliary regression after Table 2 accounts for the non-oil investment slope increase of 0.727 when schooling is omitted. Section 4 distinguishes the local income transition from the exact solution on the balanced capital mix. Figure 1’s quartile means are a defensible graphical choice because the regressions retain individual countries and the caption explains the lost dispersion.

3.evidence: Section 4 derives benchmark half-lives of 17.3 and 34.7 years. At constant returns it shows how the capital mix converges, how an initial imbalance affects eventual scale, and why stationary scales exist only at C=q. Section 5 retains country-specific population growth in the benchmark test and explains why the fitted common speed can differ from the speed at mean q. Table 5 uses full-covariance delta-method errors. Its benchmark p-values rely on homoskedasticity, a limitation the text identifies without providing a robust sensitivity check.

4.evidence: Section 2 distinguishes holding the human stock fixed from holding its investment rate fixed and derives how omitted education spending changes recorded GDP and the investment denominator. Section 6 reports a calibrated intermediate-sample net physical return averaging 12.26% with an 8.47 percentage-point standard deviation. Its separate off-steady-state exercise shows why a tenfold income gap implies gross return ratios of 100 or about 3.16 under the two benchmarks. The four historical comparisons specify the missing yields, flows, asset payments, compensation records and lifetime earnings needed to test those predictions.

summary: Adding schooling raises unrestricted adjusted income-level fit from 0.592 to 0.779 in the non-oil sample and from 0.588 to 0.771 in the intermediate sample. OECD level fit remains weaker, although unconditional catch-up is clearest there. The augmented model gives more plausible physical shares and a closer account of adjustment. The evidence stops short of establishing one parameter vector across levels and growth, and the available observations cannot validate the predicted return gaps.
recognition: The manuscript’s opening source comment discloses recognition of the general augmented growth-model exercise. This assessment uses the public question and supplied materials without a reference comparison.
